title: 2027 Corvette Grand Sport and Grand Sport X Review: Best for Last

body_markdown:
The eighth generation of the Corvette is entering its eighth model year, and like any baseball game that is winding down, it’s time to send in the closer. Welcome the Grand Sport, a Corvette model with a historical reputation as a crack relief pitcher, arriving mid-to-late-game with a list of substantial styling, power, and performance upgrades to keep the pot boiling through the last few innings. Now that we’ve driven it, we can say that the pot is properly frothing. Corvette lovers who have waited patiently for the Grand Sport will be richly rewarded with a car—actually, two cars, including the all-wheel-drive hybrid Grand Sport X—that does quite a lot, quite a lot better.


[Isaac Shapiro](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/ishapirohagerty-com/)


[Isaac Shapiro](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/ishapirohagerty-com/)


[Isaac Shapiro](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/ishapirohagerty-com/)


We’re on our third generation of the modern Grand Sport, which Corvette chief engineer Josh Holder sums up as “the sweet spot” of the Corvette lineup, offering “the stance and looks of the wide-body models with the approachability of the base engine.” In case you’ve lost track of all the puppies C8 has spawned, the top dogs are the 670-hp[Z06](https://www.hagerty.com/media/new-car-reviews/review-the-2023-chevrolet-corvette-z06-redefines-the-american-supercar/) (among the naturally aspirated variants) and the twin-turbo,[1250-hp ZR1X](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2j0DMSTZPU4) . Both receive, in addition to their various aero and power enhancements, fenders flared by 3.6 inches to package meatier meats. The Grand Sport delivers that mega-stanced look along with a few extra standard features such as magnetic-ride shocks, but with[the Stingray’s](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/2027-corvette-stingray-is-200-mph-democratized/) base 535-hp engine. That holds the GS’ starting price to $88,495 for the rear-drive coupe and $112,195 for the X, whose front electric motor and engine produce a combined 721 horsepower.


[Isaac Shapiro](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/ishapirohagerty-com/)


[Isaac Shapiro](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/ishapirohagerty-com/)


Not that the Stingray’s new base engine is a sniveling weenie. The cast-aluminum, dry-sump, 6600-rpm LS6 that goes into both the entry-level 2027 Stingray (which gets a $1000 price bump to $73,495) and Grand Sport is the racer of the new Gen 6 small-block family. Against the Stingray’s previous base engine, the 6.2-liter 495-hp LT2, the displacement rises to 6.7 liters on the back of an 8-mm stroke to an even 100 mm. With the compression ratio cranked up from 11.5 to 13:1, the LS6 makes 535 horsepower and a tire-twisting 520 pound-feet of torque, which GM claims is the most torque ever offered in a naturally aspirated V-8.


## Specs: 2027 Chevrolet Corvette Grand Sport/Grand Sport X


**Base Price:** $88,495/$112,195 (GS/GS X)
**Powertrain:** 6.7-liter V-8 (GS) with permanent magnet drive electric motor (GS X only); eight-speed dual-clutch automatic transmission
**Output:** 535 hp, 520 lb-ft torque from V-8 (GS); 186 hp and 145 lb-ft from front e-motor, 721 hp combined (GS X)
**Layout:** Mid-engine, two-door, two-passenger, rear- or all-wheel-drive targa-top coupe
**Weight:** 3520/3800 pounds (GS/GS X)
**0–60 mph:** 2.75 seconds/TBA (GS/GS X)
**EPA-rated Fuel Economy:** 15/23/17 mpg (city/highway/combined: GS); TBA (GS X)
**Competitors:** Porsche 911, Lotus Emira


[Isaac Shapiro](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/ishapirohagerty-com/)


[Isaac Shapiro](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/ishapirohagerty-com/)


[Isaac Shapiro](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/ishapirohagerty-com/)


Besides adopting a completely forged rod-and-piston assembly for strength, a dual fueling system that includes both port and direct injection, and a revised cylinder-head cooling strategy, assistant chief engineer for the small-block, Mike Kociba, tells us that the LS6’s power and fuel economy are improved and emissions reduced thanks to some counter-intuitive thinking.


For example, the increase in displacement actually reduces specific fuel consumption because turning a bigger engine slower is thriftier than making a smaller engine work harder to accomplish the same result, he says. Also, the LS6 intake runners are actually smaller in diameter than the outgoing LT2’s because improved computer modeling combined with some Corvette racing experience proved that narrower runners move air faster, more than making up for reduced volume. The recommended oil is also thicker, now 5W-50, because while thicker oil takes more energy to pump, it doesn’t mist as much as 0-weight oil in the crankcase, thus reducing the density of the air displaced internally by the pistons as they drop, which reduces parasitic losses. (It may also be that GM is changing course on 0W oil after[some highly publicized engine recalls](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/877000-gm-trucks-and-suvs-recalled-for-issues-with-the-6-2-liter-v-8/) , but Kociba won’t cop to that).


[Isaac Shapiro](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/ishapirohagerty-com/)


Because Corvette engineers are different, Kociba wanted the aluminum LS6 blocks to be cast with their displacement noted in Yankee cubic inches rather than Euro-style liters, as in the past: “We asked if there are rules about that and they said no, do whatever you want,” he explained. So, embossed next to the flywheel is the number 409, for 409 cubes. Unfortunately, to see this little Easter egg you would first have to remove the eight-speed transmission.


Haven’t we heard that LS6 name before? Indeed, we have, several times in Corvette history, most recently back in 2002 when a 405-hp V-8 bearing that designation was installed in the C5-generation Corvette Z06. Veteran Corvette development engineer Tony Roma explained that, in GM order-code-speak, L is used for all engines (F for suspensions, J for brake packages, etc.) and the Corvette team tends to recycle its codes because every time they consider a new one, they discover “it was already used on some diesel we only sold in Korea or something, so we tend to stay in our lane.” Side note: Roma recently discovered his own signature on the engineering release specs for that last LS6, 25 years ago. Once people are in the Corvette program, they tend to stay.


[Isaac Shapiro](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/ishapirohagerty-com/)


[Isaac Shapiro](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/ishapirohagerty-com/)


[Isaac Shapiro](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/ishapirohagerty-com/)


[Isaac Shapiro](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/ishapirohagerty-com/)


That kind of consistency ensures knowledge doesn’t get lost, allowing each Corvette model to build on the past. Given Chevy’s two different Grand Sport models, each with multiple driver-selectable performance modes and numerous levels in their optional Performance Traction Management systems to play with, a lot of experience goes into finessing those systems to give the driver the experience they’re looking for. With an electronic throttle, an electronic rear differential, electronic stability control, an electrified front axle on the X, plus electronic shocks, there are a ridiculous number of variables to tune in a Grand Sport. Even the feel of the electrically boosted brake system changes across the different modes; the initial bite is stronger in Touring mode than in Track mode, where drivers tend to prefer more subtle modulation.


[Isaac Shapiro](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/ishapirohagerty-com/)


[Isaac Shapiro](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/ishapirohagerty-com/)


Chevy turned us loose at the twisting, undulating Atlanta Motorsports Park to wring the necks of both Grand Sports. Swapping from Grand Sport to Grand Sport X, we found the rear-drive GS to be the most fun. It has less power and less head-snapping traction out of a corner than the X, which plays a Star Trek-like phaser noise through its speakers to tell you when the front axle is alive. But the lighter and less filtered steering, the higher overall grip, and the quicker helm response on the optional Michelin Pilot Sport Cup 2R tires, which are not available from the factory on the X, made the base Grand Sport feel more agile.


The Grand Sport X, when fitted with the Z52 Performance Package, wears Michelin Pilot Sport 4S summer rubber.


[Isaac Shapiro](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/ishapirohagerty-com/)


The rear-drive Grand Sport can be equipped with an optional Track Performance Package that adds carbon-ceramic brakes and Michelin Cup 2R tires.


[Isaac Shapiro](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/ishapirohagerty-com/)


A quad center-exit exhaust is optional—offered for the first time on a pushrod-powered C8 Corvette.


[Isaac Shapiro](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/ishapirohagerty-com/)


The quad exhaust comes with Track Package versions of the rear-drive GS, along with a Carbon Aero kit.


[Isaac Shapiro](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/ishapirohagerty-com/)


The rear-drive Grand Sport shrinks around you, while the faster but 280-pounds-heavier X, slightly hamstrung by its less aggressive Michelin Pilot Sport 4S touring tires, feels every inch the big car that the modern Corvette has become. If you’re buying a Corvette to chase apexes, the base Grand Sport is the way to go, and it’s a fabulous way to go. Besides offering Ferrari- or McLaren-level performance at a quarter of the price, it is also the only naturally aspirated mid-engine sports car in mass production with this much power. If you missed buying a 2009-2015 Ferrari 458 when it was at its depreciation nadir (the F-brand’s final non-turbo V-8 is currently—and rightly—[zooming upward in value](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/hagerty-insider/with-a-huge-spike-in-value-the-ferrari-458-speciale-is-well-special/) ), the Grand Sport is a pretty decent consolation prize. And, unlike a used 458, it comes with a warranty.


The dual hash marks, seen here on the rear fender, are a familiar Grand Sport graphics cue.


[Isaac Shapiro](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/ishapirohagerty-com/)


The electrified X’s relationship to the base Grand Sport is perhaps best likened to the relationship between the Porsche 911 Turbo and the[GT3](https://www.hagerty.com/media/video/the-drivers-seat-henry-catchpole-on-the-latest-porsche-911-gt3/) . One has the power brag and all-weather touring advantage, while the other is the track weapon. Both Corvettes assault the ears with a wicked bawl from the free-revving V-8. Though the engine sound is augmented by the car’s cockpit speakers, a lot of work went into tuning the car’s actual voice; the Grand Sport adopted an optional center exhaust (over the Stingray’s standard corner exhausts) after it proved better for giving the car a uniquely shrill snarl. Parabolic reflectors around the tailpipes send sound forward toward the cabin, where it is augmented by the sound system.


GT2 Carbon Fiber bucket seats.


[Isaac Shapiro](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/ishapirohagerty-com/)


Forged wheels wrap around carbon-ceramic rotors in the Track Performance Package.


[Isaac Shapiro](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/ishapirohagerty-com/)


When selected, the carbon brakes replace iron rotors borrowed from the Z06.


[Isaac Shapiro](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/ishapirohagerty-com/)


The aforementioned brakes, available in either iron or carbon-ceramic, deserve special call-out. Atlanta is a tight circuit that asks a lot from the stoppers, and the swing of the Grand Sport’s left pedal and the subsequent resistance levels are so natural and highly calibrated that it’s easy for the driver to plumb the deep reserves of stopping power to the exact degree they need for the situation. Over and over. Once out on the road, the Grand Sport in both flavors chills out into a fairly mellow tourer, the magnetorheological shocks that come standard on both Grand Sport models being essential to the car’s ability to both sop up road blight and keep the body under disciplined control.


[Isaac Shapiro](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/ishapirohagerty-com/)


As with a Porsche, buying a Grand Sport means wading deep into the online configurator, because even the famous Grand Sport fender hashmarks are optional. The all-important Performance Traction Management system is bundled in the Z52 Performance Package along with upgraded iron Brembo brakes and the Pilot Sport 4S summer tires, for $3500. The Z52 Track Performance Package, which is unavailable on the Grand Sport X, swaps in carbon-ceramic brakes plus some carbon exterior trim bits and Michelin Pilot Sport Cup 2R tires for a breathtaking $20,695. You’ll probably end up well over $100,000 on a Grand Sport and as high as $150,000 on X if you’re looking for maximum performance and style in both models.


We’re told the Grand Sport duo will be the final iteration of the C8 before… well …nobody will say. But likely a C9 generation that is evolutionary rather than revolutionary. We assume because the Grand Sport ushers in a new engine with just a few years left in the generation, that the same basic package will likely form the basis of a C9 coming in 2029 or so. At least, we hope so, because there’s not a lot that needs changing in this Corvette’s current form.


## 2027 Chevrolet Corvette Grand Sport and Grand Sport X


**Highs:** Ferrari/McLaren performance at a quarter of the price. New LS6 engine for both Stingray and Grand Sport. MR shocks standard. The last and probably best version of the C8.


**Lows:** Can’t option the Grand Sport X to be the same level of track animal as the Grand Sport. Still no manual transmission. If you bought an earlier C8 Corvette, your car just became obsolete.


**Takeaway:** Since the C5 generation, GM has been determined to evolve the Corvette to run with the best in the world. The C8 Grand Sport proves Detroit can do it.
